description: We are a two-person student team from Bhopal, India, competing in the NASA Space Apps Challenge. Kaustubh Gaur (Backend & ML Lead) designed and trained the PyTorch CombustionResNet model on NASA BASS-II (PSI-25) ISS data, built the FastAPI inference engine with envelope safety guards, and integrated the Qwen crew briefing pipeline. Daksh Patel (Frontend Lead) built the React and Vite web interface, interactive flame visualizer, and Vercel deployment.
summary:
NOCURA is a real-time microgravity fire-safety decision tool that predicts whether a solid-material flame will sustain itself or self-extinguish aboard a spacecraft using two cabin sensor inputs: ambient oxygen percentage and convective airflow velocity. Without gravity to drive buoyancy-based airflow, cabin ventilation fans determine whether a flame suffocates, burns steadily, or blows out.

Grounded in 51 experimental runs of 6.35 mm cast PMMA rods from NASA's Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II, PSI-25) investigation aboard the International Space Station, NOCURA uses a lightweight PyTorch residual neural network exported to pure Python for sub-millisecond edge inference via FastAPI. To ensure reliability, strict envelope guards prevent extrapolation beyond verified experimental bounds (13.5%–21.9% O₂ and 0.106–16.298 cm/s), while a separate language assistant translates verified flame states into plain-English crew actions and answers follow-up scenario questions alongside a deterministic offline fallback. The React web interface also features an interactive flame visualizer and an explorer for NASA's BASS-II, Saffire-II, SAME, and FLEX combustion datasets.
details:
What does it do and how does it work? NOCURA is a real-time spacecraft fire-safety tool that checks whether a solid-material flame will keep burning or die out on its own in microgravity using two basic cabin sensor readings: ambient oxygen percentage and airflow speed. On Earth, hot air rises and pulls fresh oxygen into a fire through gravity. In space, there is no buoyancy, so cabin ventilation fans decide everything: too little airflow starves the flame, gentle airflow feeds it oxygen so it spreads steadily, and strong airflow blows it out.

Under the hood, NOCURA uses a lightweight neural network (CombustionResNet) trained on 51 real experimental runs of 6.35 mm cast PMMA rods from NASA's Burning and Suppression of Solids - II (BASS-II, PSI-25) experiment on the International Space Station. We scaled airflow velocity logarithmically so the model captures the sharp extinction boundaries across low and high fan speeds, then exported the weights to JSON so our FastAPI backend runs pure-Python predictions in under a millisecond with zero GPU needed. Once the model locks in the flame state, a plain-English assistant explains what is physically happening inside the cabin, gives three immediate crew actions, and lets the user ask follow-up "what-if" scenario questions. The web app also includes an interactive flame visualizer and a searchable explorer comparing BASS-II with NASA's Saffire-II, SAME, and FLEX fire investigations.

What benefits does it have and what is the intended impact? Raw microgravity combustion datasets and research papers are hard to use quickly during an onboard emergency, and Earth fire rules do not work in orbit. NOCURA turns two live cabin telemetry numbers into an immediate, easy-to-read hazard assessment and actionable steps for astronauts, such as isolating local rack fans, cutting power to overheating hardware, and checking for hidden smoldering, helping crews respond faster before a small ignition spreads.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, and software did you use?

Languages & Frameworks: Python, FastAPI, PyTorch, JavaScript/TypeScript, React, and Vite.

Data & Models: NASA Physical Sciences Informatics (PSI-25 / BASS-II dataset), custom CombustionResNet exported to model_artifacts.json for deterministic edge inference, and Qwen (via Groq API) for optional plain-English crew briefings and follow-up Q&A.

Development & Deployment: Visual Studio Code, Git/GitHub, Vercel, and a standard Windows laptop. ChatGPT and Gemini were used during development to help with debugging, code cleanup, and documentation.

How is it creative and what factors did you consider? Instead of letting a large language model guess safety numbers, where hallucinations could be dangerous, we separated the physics prediction from the text explanation. The PyTorch model handles the numerical boundary strictly within NASA's tested limits (13.5%–21.9% oxygen and 0.106–16.298 cm/s airflow) and refuses to extrapolate outside that envelope. We also prioritized recall over precision during training because missing a real fire in a spacecraft (a false negative) is far worse than triggering an extra safety check. Finally, we built a live toggle on the interface to turn off the AI briefing layer and demonstrate our deterministic physics fallback so the system remains reliable even without an internet or LLM connection.
